qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture seven. The Paxos protocol. This is how a group of machines agrees on one value, even when some fail.
Two-phase commit needs all five nodes to say yes.
Two-phase commit needs all five to say yes.
If one crashes, it is stuck, waiting for the answer.
One crash and it is stuck waiting.
Paxos needs only a majority, three of five.
Paxos needs a majority: 3 of 5.
So two nodes may crash, and the rest still agree.
2 may crash.
In Paxos, a node can play three roles.
A node can play three roles.
A proposer suggests a value, here seven.
Proposers suggest a value.
Acceptors decide which value is chosen, and they all choose seven.
Acceptors decide which one is chosen.
Learners take no part. They are only told the result.
Learners are only told the result.
Every proposal carries its own number, and no two are the same.
Each proposal gets a unique number.
Proposer one uses the odd numbers, and proposer two the even ones, so they never share.
Proposers never share a number.
A bigger number means a newer proposal.
A bigger number means newer.
When two compete, the newer one beats the older, here six beats five.
The newer proposal beats the older.
A majority of five is three. We call that a quorum.
A majority of 5 is 3: a quorum.
So up to two nodes may crash.
So 2 may crash.
Any two majorities overlap. Take A, B and C, and then C, D and E.
Two majorities always overlap.
They share at least one acceptor, here C.
They share at least one acceptor.
Phase one. Acceptor E is down.
Phase 1. Acceptor E is down.
A proposer sends prepare one to all five.
PREPARE 1 goes to all.
The acceptors that hear it answer with a promise.
Acceptors answer PROMISE.
Three promises make a quorum, and here four arrive.
3 promises make a quorum.
A promise means the acceptor will ignore older proposals.
A promise: ignore older proposals.
Phase two. Now the proposer asks them to accept.
Phase 2: ask them to accept.
Accept carries the proposal number and the value.
ACCEPT carries number and value.
The acceptors that accept tell the learners.
Acceptors tell the learners.
When a majority has accepted, the value is chosen.
A majority accepted: it is chosen.
The learners are told, and the answer is seven.
The learners are told: 7.
Now two proposers collide.
Two proposers can collide.
P one asks A, B and C to promise number one.
P1 asks A, B, C to promise 1.
P two asks B, C, D and E to promise number two.
P2 asks B to E to promise 2.
B and C promised the bigger number, so they ignore P one's value.
B and C ignore the older number.
P two gets a majority, and nine is chosen.
P2 has a majority: 9 is chosen.
P one must retry, with number three.
P1 must retry with 3.
P one crashed after A and B accepted seven.
P1 crashed after A and B accepted 7.
Now P two asks B, C and D to promise number two.
P2 asks B, C, D to promise 2.
B reports the seven it accepted. C and D report nothing.
B reports the 7 it accepted.
So P two must send seven, not its own nine.
So P2 must send 7, not its own 9.
Seven stays chosen, so the value is safe.
7 stays chosen: it is safe.
A replicated system runs one Paxos round for each log entry.
Each log entry is one Paxos round.
Round one chose plus fifty, so a balance of one hundred becomes one hundred and fifty.
Round 1 chose +50: 100 → 150.
Round two chose minus twenty, which takes it to one hundred and thirty.
Round 2 chose −20: 150 → 130.
Every replica gets the same entries, in the same order.
Every replica gets the same order.
A majority decides. Three of five is enough, so two may crash.
Prepare and promise first, and then accept.
Never change a value that may already be chosen.
